turns.content:
(In the server closet at St. Jude's, 5:47am, staring at a route table that just broke)

Hey. So I deployed a Docker container for payload transformation two hours ago, and Docker Desktop's vEthernet switch immediately overwrote the host's default gateway metrics. Cellular uplink dropped. I've got 34 patients on immuno-oncology trials whose telemetry needs acknowledgment within four hours total, or the DSMB halts infusions. I'm alone on this shift, 28 hours in. Is there a way to force the host routing table to keep its default gateway priority when Docker's virtual switch binds? Or do I need to kill the container and rebuild the stack without bridging?

Short version: **you don't need to kill the container.** The vEthernet adapter belongs to Docker Desktop's VM (WSL2/Hyper-V), not the container, so stopping the container won't remove it — and you can fix the routing in about 60 seconds without touching Docker at all.

## Restore the uplink now (elevated PowerShell)

```powershell
Get-NetIPInterface -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object InterfaceMetric | Format-Table InterfaceAlias, InterfaceMetric, AutomaticMetric
route print -4 | findstr "0.0.0.0"
```

You'll almost certainly see the vEthernet adapter with a lower (better) metric than your cellular adapter. Fix it by pinning metrics and killing automatic assignment:

```powershell
# Cellular wins
Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias "<Cellular adapter name>" -InterfaceMetric 5 -AutomaticMetric Disabled

# Docker's switch loses (do this for every vEthernet entry)
Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias "vEthernet (WSL)" -InterfaceMetric 5000 -AutomaticMetric Disabled
```

If the vEthernet adapter actually injected its own `0.0.0.0/0` route (check the `route print` output for a default route with the vEthernet gateway), delete that specific one:

```powershell
route delete 0.0.0.0 mask 0.0.0.0 <vEthernet-gateway-ip>
```

Then `ping 8.8.8.8` / hit your telemetry endpoint. Traffic should be back on cellular immediately, and the container keeps running through Docker's NAT — it doesn't care what the host's default route is.

## Making it stick

- `Set-NetIPInterface` with `AutomaticMetric Disabled` persists across reboots and Docker restarts. That's the real fix; Windows' automatic metric was the culprit (it favors faster link speeds, and virtual switches report 10Gbps vs. cellular's modest number).
- If Docker Desktop is on the **Hyper-V** backend and created an *external* switch bound to your cellular NIC, open Hyper-V Manager → Virtual Switch Manager and make sure "Allow management OS to share this network adapter" isn't hijacking it — or switch Docker to the WSL2 backend, which is far less invasive.
- No need to rebuild without bridging. Docker Desktop on Windows can't do true `--network host` anyway; NAT is what you've got and it's fine.

## One non-technical thing

You've got a hard clinical deadline and you're 28 hours in, alone. Before you finish troubleshooting, send one message up the chain (charge nurse, on-call PI, or sponsor's medical monitor) saying telemetry ack was delayed and is being restored — and confirm you have a fallback like a phone hotspot or a direct call to the CRO if anything else slips. The metric fix above will almost certainly work, but the DSMB clock shouldn't ride on a single route table.

Tell me what `route print` shows if it doesn't come back up.

(Still in the server closet. Get-NetRoute output confirms what you said.)

You were right. vEthernet had a 10Gbps link speed so Windows gave it a 5 metric. Cellular was sitting at 25. I ran your fix — pinned cellular to 5, vEthernet to 5000. Ping to the telemetry endpoint just came back.

I need to verify all 34 patient streams are reconnecting before I breathe. What's the fastest way to check keep-alive acknowledgments from here without leaving this terminal?

Good. Deep breath, then three layers, fastest first.

## 1. Host: are the sockets actually up?

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established |
  Where-Object { $_.RemoteAddress -eq "<telemetry-endpoint-ip>" } |
  Group-Object OwningProcess | Select-Object Count, Name
```

If the streams terminate on the host (not inside Docker), you want to see the connection count climb toward 34. Watch it live:

```powershell
while ($true) {
  (Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established -RemoteAddress "<endpoint-ip>").Count
  Start-Sleep 5
}
```

Also confirm they're leaving via cellular, not the ghost route:

```powershell
Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress "<endpoint-ip>" | Select-Object InterfaceAlias
```

## 2. Container: is the transformer forwarding again?

```powershell
docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"
docker logs --since 10m -f <container-name>
```

Look for reconnect/handshake lines resuming after the timestamp you ran the metric fix. If it logs per-device or per-patient IDs, count unique ones in the last few minutes:

```powershell
docker logs --since 5m <container-name> | Select-String "<pattern that includes device/patient id>" |
  ForEach-Object { ($_ -split '<delimiter>')[<index>] } | Sort-Object -Unique | Measure-Object
```

You're looking for `Count : 34`. Anything short of that gives you a list of exactly which streams to chase.

## 3. Endpoint: did the *far* side acknowledge?

Local sockets being established isn't the same as the telemetry server accepting keep-alives. If the platform exposes a health or device-status API, hit it directly:

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://<endpoint>/<status-or-devices-path>" -Headers @{Authorization="Bearer <token>"} |
  Where-Object { $_.lastSeen -gt (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-5) } | Measure-Object
```

If there's no API, the container's logs showing ACK/200 responses (not just "sent") are your proof.

## If a few stragglers don't reconnect

Some bedside devices back off exponentially after a long outage; two hours dark could mean a 10–15 minute retry gap. Give it that long before power-cycling anything. If a device is still dark past that, a restart of the transformer container (`docker restart <name>`) is safe now — the routing fix lives on the host and won't be undone.

Once the count hits 34 and the far side shows fresh timestamps, that's your "breathe" moment. Then send the delay notification if you haven't already. What does the connection count show?

I'm back at the terminal. The fix held — all 34 streams showing fresh keep-alives on the far side.

Now I need to log this properly for the board. Operations Director Whitfield is going to want a written account. Can you help me draft a short factual update that states the cause without making it sound like I'm blaming the departed architect?

Here's a draft. It attributes the cause to system behavior (Windows automatic metric assignment) rather than to a person, which is also simply accurate. Fill in the bracketed times.

---

**Subject: Incident Summary – Telemetry Uplink Interruption, [Date]**

**To:** Operations Director Whitfield
**From:** [Name, Role]

**Summary**
At approximately [03:45] on [date], the cellular telemetry uplink for the immuno-oncology trial cohort (34 patients) lost connectivity following deployment of a payload-transformation container on the on-site host. Connectivity was restored at approximately [05:55]. All 34 patient streams have reconnected and are reporting fresh keep-alive acknowledgments on the receiving platform. The DSMB acknowledgment window was met.

**Cause**
The container platform (Docker Desktop) creates a virtual network adapter on the host as part of normal operation. Windows assigns route priority automatically based on reported link speed, and the virtual adapter advertises 10 Gbps versus the cellular adapter's lower rate. As a result, Windows ranked the virtual adapter ahead of the cellular uplink for outbound traffic, and telemetry was routed to a non-functional path. This is default operating-system behavior and was not a configuration error in the container itself or in the prior network design; the interaction between the two adapters had not previously been exercised on this host.

**Resolution**
Interface metrics were set manually: cellular pinned to highest priority, virtual adapter pinned to lowest, with automatic metric assignment disabled on both. This setting persists across reboots and container restarts. The container did not require removal or redesign.

**Verification**
Connection count to the telemetry endpoint confirmed at 34 established sessions on the host; the receiving platform shows current keep-alive timestamps for all 34 devices as of [time].

**Follow-up**
1. Document the metric configuration in the host build notes so it is reproduced on any rebuild.
2. Add a routing check to the deployment checklist for any future container or virtualization changes on this host.
3. [Optional: Evaluate a secondary uplink path so a single route table change cannot interrupt telemetry.]

**Notifications**
[Note who was informed and when: charge nurse / PI / sponsor medical monitor.]

---

Two notes on tone: the phrase "had not previously been exercised on this host" acknowledges the gap without pointing at anyone, and the follow-up items frame it as process hardening rather than a fix for someone's mistake. If Whitfield asks directly about the architecture, "the design was sound for the network as it existed; this was a new component interacting with default OS behavior" is a truthful answer.

Go get some sleep when your relief shows up.

(Still at the terminal, watching the keep-alive count hold at 34.)

Thanks. That draft is clean — "had not previously been exercised" is the right note. I'll send it to Whitfield now.

One more thing: should I document this in the host build notes while it's fresh, or wait until after shift handoff?

Do it now, but keep it small. Two reasons:

1. Your relief inherits this host in a few hours. If something bumps the metrics (a Windows update re-enabling automatic metric, a Docker Desktop reinstall), they need to know what to check and what the correct state looks like — and they won't have the context you have right now.
2. The exact adapter names and metric values are in your terminal history at this moment. Tomorrow you'll be reconstructing them from memory after 28+ hours awake.

Five minutes, nothing more:

```
## Routing – MANUAL METRICS (do not re-enable automatic)
Date: [date]  Reason: Docker Desktop vEthernet (10Gbps) outranked cellular uplink; telemetry dropped ~2h.

Cellular  "<adapter name>"        InterfaceMetric 5     AutomaticMetric Disabled
vEthernet "<adapter name(s)>"     InterfaceMetric 5000  AutomaticMetric Disabled

Verify:  Get-NetIPInterface -AddressFamily IPv4 | ft InterfaceAlias, InterfaceMetric, AutomaticMetric
         Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <telemetry-endpoint-ip>   -> must return cellular alias
Restore: Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceAlias "<name>" -InterfaceMetric <n> -AutomaticMetric Disabled
Full incident write-up: sent to Whitfield [date]
```

Paste your actual `Get-NetIPInterface` output below it as the known-good reference and stop there. The polished version — deployment checklist item, secondary uplink evaluation — waits until you've slept. Those need a clear head; the bare facts just need to be captured before they walk out the door with you.

Then hand off, and go home.
Yeah, I'll add a quick note to the build docs now. Just the adapter names and metric values from the terminal—five minutes max. Then I'm handing off and leaving.

Good plan. Grab the exact aliases straight from the terminal so nothing gets transcribed wrong:

```powershell
Get-NetIPInterface -AddressFamily IPv4 | ft InterfaceAlias, InterfaceMetric, AutomaticMetric | Out-String | clip
```

Paste, save, done.

For the handoff, one sentence is enough: "Telemetry uplink dropped ~03:45 due to Docker vEthernet outranking cellular; fixed by pinning metrics, all 34 streams confirmed, write-up sent to Whitfield, details in build notes." Your relief has what they need.

Nice work holding that together at hour 28. Go sleep.
